Canada: the Supreme Court upholds almost all of Quebec's law banning religious symbols for teachers, police officers and judges, and Carney vows never to use the same weapon

On Friday, November 27, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld most of Bill 21, Quebec's secularism law. Teachers, police officers, prosecutors and judges still cannot wear a hijab, turban, kippah or cross at work. The law survived by a single vote [1][3][5].

The Court upheld the law except for one article: the one requiring members of Quebec's National Assembly to sit with their faces uncovered. It found it contrary to section 3 of the Canadian Charter of Rights, which guarantees the right to vote and to run for office [1][3].
The ban covers public school teachers and principals, police officers, Crown prosecutors, government lawyers and judges while on the job [1][5].

To shield the law from challenges, Quebec had used the "notwithstanding clause" in advance: a constitutional provision that lets a legislature apply a law even if it limits certain Charter rights. Six of the seven judges found that Quebec used it validly [3][4].

Chief Justice Richard Wagner, who wrote the main opinion, said a court must "confine itself to verifying" that the formal requirements of this clause are met, because it exists to preserve parliamentary sovereignty [3].

But four judges add that courts keep the right to say, without binding effect, that such a law violates rights. In their view, sections 6 and 8 of the law infringe freedom of religion, freedom of expression and equality; the Court did not, however, issue that declaration [3].
Three of the seven judges would have struck down the core of the law on the grounds of equality between women and men [1].
Key takeaway: the country's highest court confirms that a province can shield a law in advance from most Charter rights. It is a victory for Quebec, but a very narrow decision [1][3].

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon hailed "a victory for secularism", while criticizing the part that lets judges give their opinion on a law they cannot strike down. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called it "a win for provincial rights" [4].
On the other side, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew speaks of "legislative racism", and the chair of the English Montreal School Board said he was "extremely disappointed" [4].

In Ottawa, Mark Carney replied: "We will not use the notwithstanding clause" at the federal level. He promised to "respect the independence of the judiciary" and to study the implications of a decision that had only just been released [2].

The debate resembles the one on secularism in France, but the Quebec rule goes further: it also covers teachers and judges, not just pupils. If you are thinking of working in Quebec in public education or the police, you will not be able to wear a visible religious symbol there.

General Horta N'Tam, in power in Guinea-Bissau since the coup of November 26, 2025, signed a decree on November 26, 2026 postponing the presidential and legislative elections from December 6, 2026 to November 26, 2028. He had promised a one-year transition [1][3][5].

It also wants to cut the number of MPs from 102 to 65. A constitutional referendum held in August has already strengthened the president's powers, at the expense of the semi-parliamentary system [3][4].

The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) had rejected the junta's timetable in December, demanded the release of political detainees and a short, inclusive transition, and threatened targeted sanctions [6].

The script is a familiar one: a short transition promised at the start, then a delay citing technical or financial difficulties. As one commentator notes, without a binding mechanism, a transition that has already tripled in length can be extended again [6].

For ECOWAS, it is a new challenge. The regional organization had called for a swift return to civilian rule and threatened sanctions [6]. Its response will show whether it can still carry weight against the region's military juntas.
At home, the junta is using this delay to reshape institutions before any vote: a parliament cut to 65 MPs and a president with powers strengthened by the August referendum [3][4].

General Muhoozi, son of President Yoweri Museveni, is known for provocative statements: in February last year, he threatened to seize the city of Bunia, in Ituri [6]. In March 2026, he said he was ready to leave Ugandan positions from Lubero to Mahagi, in coordination with Kinshasa [5].

Eastern DR Congo is rich in minerals (gold, tin, coltan) coveted by many armed groups and by neighboring countries. Muhoozi's posts about Walikale, a mining area, were therefore read in Kinshasa as interference [6].

Uganda's presence nevertheless remains significant: Operation Shujja continues in other areas, and Kampala has announced no withdrawal beyond Lubero [4]. The partial withdrawal can also be read as a gesture to ease the diplomatic crisis [1][3].
